'''''Malva parviflora''''' is an annual or perennial herb that is native to [[Northern Africa]], [[Southern Europe]], and [[West Asia|Western]] and [[Central Asia|Central]] Asia and is widely naturalized elsewhere.<ref name=GRIN/> Common names include cheeseweed,<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=2008-06-02}}</ref> cheeseweed mallow, Egyptian mallow,<ref name=GRIN/> least mallow,<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> little mallow,<ref name=GRIN/> mallow,<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Malva parviflora'' |id=4961 }}</ref> marshmallow,<ref name=FloraBase/> small-flowered mallow,<ref name=NSW>{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Malva  |species=parviflora }}</ref> small-flowered marshmallow,<ref name=SA>{{cite web | url = http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/texhtml.cgi?form=speciesfacts&family=Malvaceae&genus=Malva&species=parviflora | title = ''Malva parviflora'' L. | work = Electronic Flora of South Australia Fact Sheet | publisher = State Herbarium of South Australia | access-date = 2008-06-03 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150924013846/http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/texhtml.cgi?form=speciesfacts&family=Malvaceae&genus=Malva&species=parviflora | archive-date = 2015-09-24 | url-status = dead }}</ref> and smallflower mallow.<ref name=FloraBase/> It is used in [[traditional medicine]].

== Description ==
''M. parviflora'' has a decumbent or erect habit, growing up to 50–80{{nbsp}}cm in height.<ref name=NSW/><ref name="IPM" /> The broad leaves have 5–7{{nbsp}}shallow lobes and are 8–10{{nbsp}}cm in diameter.<ref name=NSW/> The lobe edges are round-toothed, with varying hairiness.<ref name="IPM" /> It has small white or pink flowers year-round at the base of leaf stalks; flowers have 4–10{{nbsp}}mm long petals.<ref name=NSW/><ref name="IPM" /> The 2{{nbsp}}mm seeds are reddish-brown and kidney-shaped.<ref name="IPM" />

Newly sprouted plants have hairless, heart-shaped [[cotyledons]] with long stalks. These cotyledons are 3–12{{nbsp}}mm long and 3–8{{nbsp}}mm wide. Stalks usually do have hairs. The first leaf is rounder and larger than the others. True leaves are round and weakly lobed with wavy, shallow-toothed edges and a red spot at the leaf base. The plant rapidly grows a deep [[taproot]].<ref name="IPM" />

''M. parviflora'' has a [[diploid]] chromosome count of 42.<ref name = FLIB/>

== Taxonomy ==
''Malva parviflora'' was described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] and published in ''Demonstrationes Plantarum in Horto Upsaliensi MDCCLIII'' on October 3, 1753.<ref name = IPNI>{{cite web |url=https://wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-0000449230-2023-12?page=1 |title= Malva parviflora |website=  WFO Plant List |access-date=31 May 2024}}</ref>

The genus name ''Malva'' is from the [[Latin]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Malva sylvestris |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/plantfinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=282568 |website=Missouri Botanical Garden |access-date=21 January 2025}}</ref> word {{lang|la|malva}} 'mallow'.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lewis |first1=Charlton T. |title=An Elementary Latin Dictionary |date=1890 |publisher=American Book Company |location=New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago |url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=malva&fromdoc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0060 |access-date=21 January 2025}}</ref> Mallow was described by [[Pliny the Elder]] in his [[Naturalis Historia]] (''20, LXXXIV'').<ref>[http://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/L/Roman/Texts/Pliny_the_Elder/20*.html B. Thayer, Pliny the Elder: the Natural History, Liber XX]</ref> The species name ''parviflora'' means 'small-flowered' and is a compound of the Latin words {{lang|la|parvus}} 'small' and {{lang|la|flores}} 'flowers'.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tamarix parviflora |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/tamarix-parviflora/#:~:text=Etymology,'%2C%20meaning%20small%2Dflowered. |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=21 January 2025}}</ref>

===Subspecies===
Two subspecies are accepted.<ref name = powo>{{cite web |title=''Malva parviflora'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:561830-1 |website=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=19 February 2025}}</ref>
*''Malva parviflora'' var. ''parviflora'' – Mediterranean basin, Sahara, [[Macaronesia]], Arabian Peninsula, and Western Asia to the Caucasus and Pakistan
*''Malva parviflora'' var. ''velutina'' {{small|(J.A.Schmidt) A.Chev.}} – [[Cape Verde Islands]] ([[Santo Antão, Cape Verde|Santo Antão Island]])

== Distribution and habitat ==
''M. parviflora'' typically grows on agricultural lands and in disturbed sites such as roadsides.<ref name="IPM">{{cite web |title=Little mallow (cheeseweed) |url=https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/WEEDS/little_mallow.html |website=UC IPM |publisher=Regents of the University of California |access-date=17 May 2023}}</ref> Its native range extends from the Mediterranean, through West Asia, and to Central Asia and can be found in Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia, Kuwait, Afghanistan, Cyprus, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Greece, Croatia, Italy, Malta, Spain, France, and Portugal. The species is widely naturalized elsewhere,<ref name=GRIN/> including in [[North America]] since the 19th century.<ref name = produce/> It is a [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] weed in Australia.<ref name="manyauthors">{{cite journal |last1=Sharifi-Rad |first1=Javad |last2=Melgar-Lalanne |first2=Guiomar |last3=Hernández-Álvarez |first3=Alan Javier |last4=Taheri |first4=Yasaman |last5=Shaheen |first5=Shabnum |last6=Kregiel |first6=Dorota |last7=Antolak |first7=Hubert |last8=Pawlikowska |first8=Ewelina |last9=Brdar-Jokanović |first9=Milka |last10=Rajkovic |first10=Jovana |last11=Hosseinabadi |first11=Tahereh |last12=Ljevnaić-Mašić |first12=Branka |last13=Baghalpour |first13=Navid |last14=Mohajeri |first14=Maryam |last15=Fokou |first15=Patrick Valere Tsouh |last16=Martins |first16=Natália |title=''Malva'' species: Insights on its chemical composition towards pharmacological applications |journal=[[Phytotherapy Research]] |date=11 November 2019 |doi=10.1002/ptr.6550}}</ref>

== Toxicity ==

''M. parviflora'' accumulates pollutants such as [[cadmium]] and [[chromium]].<ref name="manyauthors"/> In nitrogen-rich soils,<ref name="produce">{{cite web |title=Foraged Mallow (Cheeseweed) |url=https://specialtyproduce.com/produce/Foraged_Mallow_Cheeseweed_10423.php |website=Specialty Produce |access-date=31 May 2024}}</ref> the plant's leaves and seeds can be toxic to cattle and poultry due to an accumulation of nitrates.<ref name="IPM" /> If consumed in large amounts, the plant can damage [[energy homeostasis]] in horses, possibly due to its [[cyclopropene]] fatty acids.<ref name="manyauthors"/>

== Uses ==
The entire plant is edible and can be eaten both raw and cooked. It has a mild flavor similar to [[chard]] and a mild, earthy aroma.<ref name = produce/>

''M. parviflora'' has been used in [[infusion]]s, [[decoction]]s, and [[poultice]]s as part of [[traditional medicine]].<ref name="FLIB">{{Cite web |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/03_060_09_Malva.pdf |title=Malva |website=Flora Iberica |access-date=2024-05-20}}</ref> In [[Mexico]], ''M. parviflora'' is consumed as a [[quelite (disambiguation)|quelite]] and used in traditional medicine to treat wounds and problems with digestion.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://132.248.9.195/ptd2005/00322/0343654/Index.html |title=Análisis biodirigido de Malva parviflora para validar su uso tradicional como auxiliar en el tratamiento de la gastritis |date=2005-04-29 |access-date=2024-05-20 |last=Mendiola Almaraz |first=Lorena}}</ref> In the 20th century, naturalist {{ill|Alfonso Herrera Fernández|lt=Alfonso Herrera Fernández|es|Alfonso Herrera Fernández}} noted that the dried leaves were used in moisturizing poultices and that the flowers were used in infusions to induce perspiration.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.medicinatradicionalmexicana.unam.mx/apmtm/termino.php?l=3&t=malva-parviflora |title=Malva |website=Biblioteca digital de la medicina tradicional mexicana |language=Spanish |access-date=2024-05-20}}</ref> Particularly in [[Zapotitlán, Puebla]], the roots are used in infusions to treat [[dysentery]]. In [[Jordan]], the leaves are used in infusions and poultices as an [[emollient]], [[laxative]], [[carminative]], and anti-[[hemorrhoid]]. In [[Lebanon]], the leaves are used in decoctions to treat [[catarrh]]s, [[kidney]] infections, [[kidney stone]]s, [[respiratory infection]]s, and [[constipation]]. In [[Ethiopia]], the roots are used to treat [[asthma]] and wounds.<ref name="manyauthors"/>

Few clinical trials have tested the efficacy of ''M. parviflora's'' traditional uses. Preclinical studies have found that extracts from various parts of the plant have [[antimicrobial]] and [[antifungal]] properties. However, this effect is usually weaker than that of standard [[antibiotic]]s. The roots and leaves have [[antioxidant]] and [[anti-inflammatory]] properties. The plant may have an [[Diabetes medication|anti-diabetic]] effect, but the effect's strength is disputed. In [[Laboratory mouse|mice]], ''M. parviflora'' extracts have shown potential to treat [[hypertension]] and [[Alzheimer's]].<ref name="manyauthors"/>
